title: Selling under your own name: how a merchant commerce platform works
audience: A curious adult coming from a different field who has never run a shop online. No knowledge of retail, payments, or software is assumed.
scope: An introduction to platforms that let independent merchants run their own branded shop online and in person, using Shopify as the best-known example. It follows one order from a shopper's first visit to the merchant being paid, and covers the platform's role in checkout, payments, stock, shipping, and its ecosystem of add-on apps. Marketplaces where the platform sells to the shopper itself (such as Amazon's retail business), warehouse operations, and detailed tax or customs law are outside this guide. Payment rules, taxes, and import duties differ by country; examples that depend on them are marked as local. The shop, people, and numbers in the walkthrough are fictional.
learningGoals: Explain why a merchant would rent a commerce platform instead of building a shop or selling only on a marketplace.
Distinguish the merchant of record from the platform, and an authorized payment from money actually paid out.
Follow one order from discovery to payout, and explain why stock shared between an online shop and a market stall can cause trouble.
Describe how the platform earns money and where its interests and the merchant's can pull apart.
Explain why fraud, shared stock, and new sales channels such as AI assistants are hard problems rather than simple features.

introduction.whatItIs: Imagine you make ceramic mugs and want strangers to buy them. You need a place where they can see the mugs, a way to take their money safely, a record of who ordered what, a way to know how many mugs you have left, and a way to get a parcel to their door. A merchant commerce platform rents you all of that as one connected service, under your own shop name and web address, for a monthly fee plus a cut of each sale.
introduction.whyItMatters:
Before such platforms, selling online meant either hiring developers to build and secure a shop, or selling inside someone else's marketplace where the marketplace owns the customer relationship. A platform lets a one-person business look and work like a much larger retailer, and lets a large retailer avoid running its own shop software.

The visible part is the shop page. The larger job is making each promise to a shopper dependable: the price is right, the item exists, the payment is safe, the parcel arrives, and the merchant is paid.
introduction.familiarComparison: Think of a shopping-mall landlord who also provides the shop fittings, the tills, the security guards, and a delivery desk. You rent a unit, put up your own sign, and focus on your products.
introduction.whereComparisonBreaks: A mall landlord brings foot traffic; a commerce platform mostly does not. Shoppers arrive because the merchant attracted them, through social media, search, ads, or word of mouth. The platform is also involved in every payment, so unlike a landlord it sees each sale, takes a share of it, and can hold back money when something looks wrong.

participants.name: The merchant
participants.role: Owns the brand and products, sets prices, and is legally the seller. Ranges from a single founder working from home to a large retailer with hundreds of stores.
participants.caresAbout: Turning visitors into paying customers, keeping fees and fraud losses low, getting paid quickly, and spending less time on admin. Larger merchants also care about connecting to their existing stock and accounting systems.

participants.name: The shopper
participants.role: Buys from the merchant, often on a phone, and often having arrived from a social media post, a search result, or an AI assistant's suggestion.
participants.caresAbout: A quick and trustworthy checkout, an accurate delivery promise, easy returns, and not having to type card and address details again.

participants.name: The platform
participants.role: Runs the shop software, checkout, and order records for millions of merchants, and usually also processes payments. It is not the seller of the goods.
participants.caresAbout: Merchants growing and staying, because its income rises with their sales. It must also keep fraud and failed payments low across the whole network.

participants.name: Payment and delivery partners
participants.role: Card networks, banks, and payment processors move the money; carriers move the parcels. The platform connects to them on the merchant's behalf.
participants.caresAbout: Their own rules and fees. A card network can fine or cut off merchants with too many disputed payments; a carrier charges by weight, distance, and speed.

participants.name: App developers and agencies
participants.role: Independent companies that build add-ons (for reviews, subscriptions, loyalty points, and much more) or design and run shops for merchants.
participants.caresAbout: Reaching merchants through the platform's app store and being paid reliably. They depend on the platform not changing its rules or copying their product.

concepts.meaning: The pages a shopper sees: the home page, product pages, and cart, shown under the merchant's own name and web address.
concepts.example: A shopper visiting the mug maker's web address sees her logo and photos, not the platform's brand, even though the platform serves every page.
concepts.whyItMatters: The merchant keeps the customer relationship and the brand. The platform stays mostly in the background, unlike a marketplace where shoppers think of themselves as buying from the marketplace.

media.title: Storefront
media.alt: Left: a merchant's own branded shop page for Mug Maker's Mugs, with the platform shown only as a small gear behind it. Right: the same mug listed in a large marketplace app, where the shopper thinks of the marketplace brand.
media.caption: On their own storefront the merchant's brand is what shoppers see. In a marketplace, the marketplace's brand comes first.

concepts.meaning: The steps where a shopper confirms what they are buying, gives a delivery address, sees the final price including shipping and tax, and pays.
concepts.example: A shopper adds two mugs, is shown a shipping charge and sales tax for her address, and pays with a saved card in one tap.
concepts.whyItMatters: Many shoppers abandon purchases here, so each extra field or surprise cost loses sales. Checkout is also where security rules for card details apply most strictly, which is one reason merchants prefer the platform to run it.

media.title: Checkout
media.alt: Left: a frustrated shopper facing a long form on a desktop, ending in an abandoned cart. Right: the same shopper paying in one tap on a phone with shipping and tax already shown, ending in a confirmed purchase.
media.caption: Every extra field and surprise cost at checkout loses buyers. A short, trusted checkout keeps them.

concepts.meaning: The business that is legally selling the goods and is responsible for refunds, taxes, and the promise made to the shopper.
concepts.example: When a mug arrives broken, the shopper's claim is against the mug maker, not against the platform that ran the checkout.
concepts.whyItMatters: It explains who answers for what. The platform provides tools and processes the payment, but the merchant carries the commercial and legal responsibility for the sale.
concepts.illustrationPrompt: Show a shopper holding a parcel with a cracked bowl, an arrow labeled 'refund request' going to a small ceramics studio labeled 'Merchant (seller)'. In the background, a separate building labeled 'Platform' with a dashed line to the studio labeled 'tools and payments'. The platform must clearly not be the one receiving the complaint.

media.title: Merchant of record
media.alt: A shopper holding a cracked bowl sends a refund request to the merchant's shop. The platform's building sits apart, linked to the shop only by a dashed line labeled tools and payments.
media.caption: The complaint goes to the seller. The platform provides tools and payments but is not the party selling the bowl.

concepts.meaning: Authorization is the shopper's bank agreeing that the money is available and setting it aside. Capture is the merchant actually claiming it, usually when the order ships. Payout is the platform sending the collected money, minus fees, to the merchant's bank account some days later.
concepts.example: A card is authorized for 60 dollars on Monday, captured on Tuesday when the parcel ships, and paid out to the merchant on Thursday as part of a batch.
concepts.whyItMatters: A successful payment on screen is not money in the merchant's bank. Between those moments the sale can still be refunded, disputed, or held for review.
concepts.illustrationPrompt: A left-to-right timeline with three distinct stages: 'Authorized' (bank sets money aside, coin in a locked box at the shopper's bank), 'Captured' (parcel leaves the studio, coin moves to the platform), 'Paid out' (days later, a smaller stack reaches the merchant's bank after a 'fees' slice is removed). Show a side branch from the first two stages labeled 'refund or dispute possible'.

media.title: Authorization, capture, and payout
media.alt: A three-stage timeline. Authorized: money locked at the shopper's bank. Captured: the parcel is handed to a courier and money moves to the platform. Paid out: a fees slice is removed before the rest reaches the merchant's bank. A refund or dispute can happen during the first two stages.
media.caption: Three different moments. Money is only the merchant's once it is paid out, and even then a later dispute can reverse it.

concepts.meaning: A disputed payment that the shopper's bank reverses, taking the money back from the merchant, often weeks after the sale.
concepts.example: Someone uses a stolen card to buy mugs. The real cardholder disputes the charge; the merchant loses the money and the mugs, and pays a dispute fee.
concepts.whyItMatters: The person who placed the order is not always the person who pays in the end. Fraud checks before shipping exist to avoid this delayed loss.

media.title: Chargeback
media.alt: Three panels: someone buys mugs with a stolen card and the merchant ships them; the real cardholder disputes the charge with their bank; the bank takes the money back from the merchant plus a fee, and the mugs are gone.
media.caption: A chargeback arrives weeks after the sale, which is why fraud checks happen before shipping. The amounts are illustrative.

concepts.meaning: Inventory is the stock the merchant holds and where it is. Availability is whether a specific item can actually be promised to a specific shopper now.
concepts.example: The merchant has three blue bowls: two in her studio and one on her market stall. Online, only the two in the studio can be shipped tomorrow.
concepts.whyItMatters: Selling the same last item twice, online and in person, forces a cancellation and an apology. Keeping one shared count across every place a sale can happen is harder than it sounds.
concepts.illustrationPrompt: One shelf in the center holding a single blue bowl, with ONE label above it: 'Shared stock: 1 blue bowl'. Two arrows from the shelf lead to two sales points trying to sell it within seconds: left, a phone website checkout with a green check and the label 'Sold first (10:01:03)'; right, a market stall card reader with a polite notice 'Item sold out (10:01:05)' and the label 'Sale stopped: no stock left'. Do not show any card being declined; the card is fine, the bowl is simply gone.

media.title: Inventory and availability
media.alt: One blue bowl on a shared shelf. An online shopper buys it at 10:01:03 and sees Sold first. At 10:01:05 the market stall's reader reports Item sold out, and the sale is stopped.
media.caption: A shared stock count lets the first recorded sale claim the last item, so nobody is sold a bowl that no longer exists.

concepts.meaning: Any place where a shopper can buy: the merchant's own website, a physical till, a social media shop, a marketplace listing, or an AI assistant.
concepts.example: The same mug is listed on the merchant's site, sold from her market stall using a card reader, and shown inside an AI chat when someone asks for a handmade gift.
concepts.whyItMatters: Each channel has its own rules and costs, but the merchant wants one catalog, one stock count, and one list of orders. Connecting channels is a large part of the platform's value.
concepts.illustrationPrompt: A single catalog of ceramic mugs in the center connected to five places a shopper can buy: 'Website', 'Market stall till', 'Social media shop', 'Marketplace', 'AI assistant chat'. All lines return to one shared 'Orders' list and one 'Stock' count.

media.title: Sales channel
media.alt: A single catalog of mugs feeds five channels: website, market stall till, social media shop, marketplace and AI assistant chat. Orders from all of them flow into one orders list and one stock count, shown dropping from 50 to 47.
media.caption: Many places to buy, but one catalog, one list of orders and one stock count behind them.

concepts.meaning: The collection of independent add-ons that merchants install from the platform's app store to extend their shop.
concepts.example: The mug maker installs a reviews app and a gift-wrap app. Each is built by a different company and billed through her platform invoice.
concepts.whyItMatters: No single platform can build every feature every merchant wants. The ecosystem fills the gaps, but it also means a merchant's shop depends on several companies at once.

media.title: App ecosystem
media.alt: A mug shop built on the platform's core features, with a reviews app and a gift wrap app from two different companies plugged in from the platform's app store. All of them appear on one monthly platform invoice.
media.caption: Outside developers fill the gaps in the platform. The merchant installs and pays for apps in one place, but their shop now depends on several companies.

historyNote: These turning points explain present practices, with Shopify used as the example platform. Other platforms followed different paths, and earlier hosted shop builders existed before it.

history.change: Mail-order catalogs, then telephone ordering, let sellers reach distant buyers without a shop in every town. Merchants still had to handle payment, stock, and shipping themselves.
history.whyItMatters: The basic chain of a remote sale, from promise to payment to delivery, is old. Online selling changed who could afford to run it, not what had to be done.

history.change: Web shops appeared, but most were custom-built or assembled from software the merchant had to host and secure. Large marketplaces offered an easier route at the cost of owning the customer relationship.
history.whyItMatters: This set up the choice that remains today: build it yourself, sell inside a marketplace, or rent a platform that sits in between.

history.change: The major card brands jointly published the Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard (PCI DSS), a common set of security rules for anyone storing, processing, or transmitting card details.
history.whyItMatters: Handling card data safely became a demanding compliance job. That made it more attractive for small merchants to let a platform run checkout and carry most of that burden.

history.change: Shopify's founders built software to sell snowboards online, found the software more useful than the shop, and launched it as a hosted platform in 2006. In 2009 they opened it to outside developers through an app store.
history.whyItMatters: The model of renting shop software by the month, with independent developers extending it, became the template for many platforms that followed.

history.change: Platforms added their own payment processing, card readers for physical shops, saved-wallet checkouts, and versions for large retailers. Shopping moved heavily to phones.
history.whyItMatters: The platform shifted from selling software to taking part in every transaction. Payments became a major source of its income and gave it a view of fraud across many merchants.

history.change: The United States ended the duty-free exemption for low-value imported parcels from all countries.
history.whyItMatters: Merchants shipping small orders into the US suddenly faced duties and customs paperwork on parcels that used to pass freely. It shows how a rule outside the platform's control can change a merchant's costs overnight.

history.change: AI assistants began recommending and buying products inside a conversation. In January 2026 Google and Shopify announced the Universal Commerce Protocol, an open standard for letting AI systems check out from merchants; a rival protocol from OpenAI and Stripe also exists.
history.whyItMatters: A new sales channel appeared where the shopper may never visit the merchant's site. Platforms must give assistants accurate products, prices, and stock while keeping the merchant as the seller.

walkthrough.title: Two mugs, a market stall, and the last blue bowl (fictional)
walkthrough.setup: Lena runs a one-person ceramics brand from her studio. She uses a commerce platform for her website, takes card payments at a weekend market with the platform's card reader, and has installed a reviews app. Sam, a shopper in another city, sees a video of her blue bowls on social media. Lena, Sam, and all amounts are invented for illustration.

steps.title: Sam arrives at the storefront
steps.whatHappens: Sam taps the link in the video and lands on Lena's product page. The page shows photos, the price, reviews from earlier buyers, and that one blue bowl is left. The platform served the page quickly on a phone and the reviews app supplied the ratings.
steps.whyItMatters: Lena paid for the visit with her own marketing. The platform's job is not to wreck that effort with a slow page or a confusing layout.

steps.title: Sam goes to checkout
steps.whatHappens: Sam adds the blue bowl and two mugs. At checkout the platform recognizes Sam's phone number from a saved wallet used at another shop on the same platform, fills in the address and card, and shows shipping and sales tax for that address. Total: 92 dollars.
steps.whyItMatters: Sam never typed a card number, which raises the chance the sale completes. Tax and shipping are calculated by the platform, but Lena, as merchant of record, is still responsible for them being right.
steps.watchOut: A surprise shipping cost at this step is one of the most common reasons shoppers give up.

steps.title: The payment is authorized and checked
steps.whatHappens: Sam's bank authorizes 92 dollars. In parallel, the platform's fraud checks compare the order with patterns seen across many merchants: is this card, device, and address combination normal? The order is scored low-risk and marked paid.
steps.whyItMatters: Authorization reserves Sam's money; it has not reached Lena. The fraud check protects Lena from a chargeback weeks later, which a single small merchant could not judge well from her own few orders.

steps.title: The exception: the last bowl sells twice
steps.whatHappens: At the same moment, Lena's friend is minding the market stall, where the one remaining blue bowl is on display. A visitor buys it with the card reader. Because the stall and the website share one stock count, whichever sale is recorded first claims the bowl. The website sale was recorded a few seconds earlier, so the reader warns that the bowl is sold, and Lena's friend apologizes and offers a different bowl.
steps.whyItMatters: Without a shared count, both sales would succeed and one customer would get a cancellation days later. Shared stock across channels is valuable precisely because these collisions happen.
steps.watchOut: Shared counting only works if every channel records sales promptly. A till working offline with a bad connection can still oversell, and someone must decide which customer to disappoint.

steps.title: Lena packs and ships
steps.whatHappens: Lena sees the order in her admin screen, buys a discounted shipping label through the platform, and prints it. Marking the order shipped captures the payment and sends Sam a tracking link.
steps.whyItMatters: Capture happens at shipping so Sam is not charged for something that never leaves. The carrier now holds the delivery promise, but Sam will still blame Lena if it is late.

steps.title: Lena is paid
steps.whatHappens: Two days later the platform pays out Lena's week of sales in one transfer. From Sam's 92 dollars it has subtracted a payment processing fee, and the shipping label cost was billed separately. Lena's monthly subscription and her reviews app appear on a separate platform bill.
steps.whyItMatters: Lena's real margin depends on all these deductions together. Payout timing also matters: a small business may need this week's sales to buy next week's clay.

walkthrough.outcome: Sam receives the bowl and mugs, leaves a review that will help the next shopper decide, and is now in Lena's customer list for future emails. Lena earned a sale she could not have handled alone, and avoided a double sale. The platform earned fees from the subscription, the payment, and the shipping label, and its fraud checks learned from one more normal order. Success for everyone means the same thing: the promise made on the product page was kept.
walkthrough.illustrationPrompt: A six-panel comic strip in reading order, same two characters throughout (Lena the ceramicist with hair in a bun and an apron; Sam the shopper with curly hair). 1 Sam on a phone sees a video of a blue bowl, label 'One blue bowl left'. 2 Sam's phone checkout with saved wallet, label 'Total $92'. 3 Shopper's bank icon 'Authorized' and a shield 'Fraud check: low risk'. 4 Complication: at a market stall, Lena's friend shows a card reader reading 'Sold online' to a visitor and offers a different bowl. 5 Lena packs the bowl and two mugs and prints a shipping label, label 'Shipped = payment captured'. 6 Two days later Lena checks her phone, label 'Payout: this week's sales minus fees'. No other numbers or amounts anywhere except $92.

media.title: Two mugs, a market stall, and the last blue bowl (fictional)
media.alt: Six comic panels: Sam sees the last blue bowl on a phone; checks out for $92; the bank authorizes and a fraud check reads low risk; at the market stall the reader shows the bowl was sold online; Lena packs the order and ships it, capturing payment; days later Lena sees a payout of the week's sales minus fees.
media.caption: The six walkthrough steps in order. In panel four the bowl is nearly sold twice, and the shared stock count stops the second sale.

valueAndIncentives.title: Who pays, and for what
valueAndIncentives.explanation: Merchants pay a monthly subscription for the software, a percentage plus a small fixed amount on each card payment, and optional extras such as shipping labels, loans, or premium support. App developers pay the platform a share of what merchants pay them. Shoppers usually pay nothing directly to the platform.
valueAndIncentives.example: For Lena, the subscription is a fixed cost; the payment fee grows with every sale. In Shopify's case, the merchant services tied to sales, payments above all, bring in most of its revenue, not the subscriptions.

valueAndIncentives.title: Aligned interests: the platform grows when merchants sell more
valueAndIncentives.explanation: Because most income scales with sales, the platform benefits from faster checkouts, better fraud decisions, and new channels that bring merchants more customers.
valueAndIncentives.example: A saved wallet that lets Sam pay in one tap helps Lena sell, helps the platform earn a fee, and saves Sam time.

valueAndIncentives.title: Where interests pull apart
valueAndIncentives.explanation: The platform may favor its own payment service, apps, or features over alternatives a merchant would prefer. It may hold back payouts when fraud risk rises, which protects the network but can starve a small business of cash. App developers fear that the platform will build a feature that replaces their app.
valueAndIncentives.example: A merchant using an outside payment provider may pay an extra platform fee on each sale, a setting that steers merchants toward the platform's own payments.

valueAndIncentives.title: Network effects across merchants
valueAndIncentives.explanation: Some benefits come from the platform serving many merchants at once: a shopper's saved wallet works at every shop, fraud signals are learned from millions of orders, and shipping rates are negotiated in bulk.
valueAndIncentives.example: Lena got a lower shipping price than she could have negotiated alone, and Sam's wallet worked on her shop the first time Sam visited.

valueAndIncentives.title: Signs of success
valueAndIncentives.explanation: Useful signs include how many visitors become buyers, how many merchants stay and grow from year to year, the share of sales paid through the platform's own payments, fraud and chargeback rates, and how quickly merchants are paid. Platforms also watch total sales across all merchants, often called gross merchandise volume, because their income follows it.
valueAndIncentives.example: If merchants leave after their first year, a platform with a growing sign-up count can still be shrinking in the way that matters.

challenges.title: Stopping fraud without blocking good shoppers
challenges.whyHard: Fraudsters test stolen cards on small shops, and chargebacks arrive weeks after the parcel has gone. The platform must decide in a fraction of a second, on limited information, whether to accept an order.
challenges.tradeOff: Stricter checks reduce losses but also reject real customers, who rarely retry. Looser checks win sales but leave merchants with chargebacks and fees.
challenges.example: A first-time buyer with a new phone, a gift address, and an expensive order looks like fraud and also like a genuine holiday shopper.
challenges.commonApproach: Score each order using patterns across all merchants, flag uncertain ones for the merchant to review, and offer protection where the platform covers approved orders that later turn out fraudulent. The limits: shared scoring can treat unusual but honest businesses unfairly, and the merchant may not understand why an order was blocked.

challenges.title: One stock count across many channels
challenges.whyHard: The same item can be sold on the website, at a till, in a social media shop, on a marketplace, and through an AI assistant, each recording sales at slightly different times and some working offline.
challenges.tradeOff: Holding stock back for each channel avoids overselling but leaves items unsold in one place while another runs out. Pooling it sells more but risks selling the same item twice.
challenges.example: Lena's last blue bowl: the shared count saved one customer from a cancellation, but only because both sales were recorded within seconds.
challenges.commonApproach: Keep a central count, reserve stock at checkout, and let merchants set safety buffers per channel. The limits: buffers waste stock, and connections to outside channels may update only every few minutes.

challenges.title: Serving a founder and a large retailer with the same product
challenges.whyHard: A new merchant needs things simple and cheap. A large retailer needs custom workflows, links to its existing systems, many countries, and wholesale prices for business buyers.
challenges.tradeOff: Every option added for large merchants can make the product more confusing for small ones. Building separately for each risks two products that drift apart.
challenges.example: A wholesale price list that hides retail prices from business buyers is essential to a large retailer and irrelevant to Lena.
challenges.commonApproach: Keep one core platform with tiered plans and let apps and agencies supply specialized needs. The limits: large merchants may still outgrow it, and many installed apps can slow shops and complicate support.

challenges.title: Selling through AI assistants
challenges.whyHard: When an assistant recommends and buys a product inside a conversation, the shopper may never see the merchant's site. The assistant needs accurate prices, stock, shipping, and return terms, and the merchant must still be the seller responsible for the sale.
challenges.tradeOff: Opening products to assistants can bring new buyers, but the merchant gives up some control over presentation and the relationship, and competing protocols mean extra work to be present everywhere.
challenges.example: Someone asks an assistant for a handmade blue bowl under 50 dollars. If the assistant shows Lena's bowl after it has already sold, the shopper is let down and may blame Lena.
challenges.commonApproach: Publish a structured, frequently updated product catalog, support open checkout protocols, and keep the payment and order recorded in the merchant's own system. The limits: standards are new and still changing, and the assistant decides which products to show.

challenges.title: Rules that change from outside
challenges.whyHard: Taxes, import duties, card network rules, and privacy laws differ by country and can change quickly. Merchants rely on the platform to keep up, but they remain legally responsible.
challenges.tradeOff: Automating tax and duty calculations helps small merchants, but every country added is ongoing work and an exposure if it is wrong.
challenges.example: When the United States ended duty-free entry for low-value parcels in 2025, merchants abroad had to decide whether to collect duties at checkout or let shoppers face surprise charges at delivery.
challenges.commonApproach: Build tax and duty calculation into checkout and update rules centrally. The limits: the merchant must still register, file, and answer to authorities, and coverage for smaller countries can lag.

misconceptions.belief: The platform sells the products, so it handles complaints.
misconceptions.reality: The merchant is the seller of record. The platform provides tools and usually processes the payment, but the shopper's claim is against the merchant.

misconceptions.belief: Having an online shop brings customers.
misconceptions.reality: A platform mostly does not bring shoppers to a merchant. Merchants usually attract visitors themselves through social media, search, ads, or word of mouth; the platform turns those visitors into orders.

misconceptions.belief: Once the payment succeeds, the money is the merchant's.
misconceptions.reality: An approved payment can still be refunded, disputed as a chargeback, or held for review. Money reaches the merchant's bank only at payout, minus fees.

misconceptions.belief: Stock is just a number you type in.
misconceptions.reality: Stock exists in places and is promised across several channels at once. Keeping that promise accurate when sales happen simultaneously is a real coordination problem.

takeaways: A merchant commerce platform rents merchants the whole chain of selling (storefront, checkout, payments, stock, shipping, and add-ons) under the merchant's own brand.
The merchant remains the seller and carries responsibility; the platform is the infrastructure and is paid mainly in proportion to sales.
A sale is a series of promises: the item exists, the price is right, the payment is genuine, the parcel arrives. Most difficulty lies in keeping those promises at the moments they are tested.
Payment is not one moment: authorization, capture, payout, and possible chargeback happen at different times, with risk between them.
New channels such as AI assistants change where shoppers buy, but not who is responsible for the sale.

knowledgeChecks.question: Sam's bowl arrives cracked. Who should Sam ask for a refund, and why?
knowledgeChecks.explanation: Lena is the merchant of record. The platform ran the checkout and processed the payment, but it did not sell the bowl, so the commercial promise and the refund obligation are Lena's.

knowledgeChecks.question: Lena's admin screen shows a paid order on Monday. Why might she still not have that money on Friday?
knowledgeChecks.answer: Paid on screen means authorized or captured, not paid out.
knowledgeChecks.explanation: The money reaches her bank only in a later payout, minus fees. In between, the order could be refunded, disputed as a chargeback, or held if fraud risk looks high.

knowledgeChecks.question: Why did the market stall's card reader refuse to sell the last blue bowl, and what would have happened without that?
knowledgeChecks.answer: The website and the stall shared one stock count, and the website sale was recorded first.
knowledgeChecks.explanation: Without a shared count both sales would have succeeded, and one customer would later have received a cancellation. Sharing stock across channels prevents that, but only if each channel records sales promptly.

knowledgeChecks.question: A platform makes most of its money from fees on each sale rather than subscriptions. Name one way this helps merchants and one way it can work against them.
knowledgeChecks.answer: It rewards the platform for helping merchants sell more, but it can also push the platform to steer merchants toward its own paid services.
knowledgeChecks.explanation: Faster checkout and better fraud decisions raise both the merchant's sales and the platform's fees. The same incentive can lead to extra fees for using an outside payment provider, or holding payouts to protect the network at a small merchant's expense.

knowledgeChecks.question: An AI assistant recommends Lena's bowl after it has sold out. What does this tell you about selling through assistants?
knowledgeChecks.answer: The assistant needs accurate, frequently updated stock and price information from the merchant's system.
knowledgeChecks.explanation: The shopper never visits Lena's site, so the assistant's information is the only promise they see. Stale data creates a broken promise that the shopper will attribute to Lena, the seller.

nextQuestions: Of all your sales, how much is lost to fraud and chargebacks, and how much do your fraud checks block by mistake?
How long after a sale does money actually reach your bank, and has a payout ever been held?
Which channels do you sell through, and how often have you sold an item you did not have?
Which apps would break your business if they disappeared tomorrow?
What share of your sales now starts from social media, search, or an AI assistant rather than people typing your address?

media.title: The people involved
media.alt: A relationship map with the merchant in the center. The shopper buys from the merchant and pays through payment partners. The platform provides shop software, checkout and payouts in return for subscription and fees. App developers supply add-ons and pay the platform a revenue share. A carrier takes the parcel from the merchant to the shopper. Green arrows are money and blue arrows are goods or services.
media.caption: Who provides what, and where money flows. Payment partners actually pass the shopper's money on to the platform and then the merchant; the map simplifies that step.
